AUM: Assets Under Management — the total market value of everything the fund holds. A rough proxy for how trusted/liquid a fund is; bigger AUM usually means tighter spreads and less risk the fund gets shut down.
Expense Ratio: The fund's annual management fee, as a % of your investment, deducted automatically from returns. 0.03% means $3/year per $10,000 invested. The single biggest controllable cost in passive investing.
NAV: Net Asset Value — the per-share value of everything the fund holds, calculated once per day after market close. An ETF's trading price can drift slightly above (premium) or below (discount) its NAV during the day.
Premium/Discount: How far an ETF's market price has drifted from its NAV. Large or persistent premiums/discounts usually signal thin liquidity or a stressed underlying market (common in international or fixed-income ETFs during volatile periods).
Beta: A measure of how much a fund moves relative to the overall market (here, the S&P 500). Beta of 1.0 moves in lockstep with the market; 1.5 means it tends to swing 50% more than the market in either direction; 0.5 means it's less volatile than the market.
Volatility: How much a fund's price swings around, measured as the annualized standard deviation of daily returns. Higher volatility means bigger day-to-day price swings, up or down — it's a measure of risk, not direction.
Sharpe Ratio: Return earned per unit of risk taken: (return − risk-free rate) ÷ volatility. Higher is better — it tells you whether a fund's returns are worth the bumpiness required to get them, not just whether it went up.
Max Drawdown: The largest peak-to-trough decline the fund has experienced in the lookback window. If a fund fell 30% from its high before recovering, that's a 30% max drawdown — a gut-check for how much pain a holder had to sit through.
Tracking Error: How closely a fund follows its benchmark index. Low tracking error means the fund does what it says on the tin. Note: this figure is computed against a price-only index feed (no dividends included), so it runs a bit higher than a fund's official tracking error vs. its true total-return benchmark — read it as directionally useful, not a precise regulatory figure.
Bid-Ask Spread: The gap between the highest price a buyer will pay (bid) and the lowest price a seller will accept (ask). A core liquidity metric on a trading desk — tighter spreads mean cheaper, easier execution, especially in size.
Average Daily Volume: The average number of shares traded per day. Higher volume generally means better liquidity and tighter spreads; low-volume ETFs can be expensive or slow to trade in large size.
Authorized Participant: A large broker-dealer contractually authorized to create and redeem large blocks ("creation units") of ETF shares directly with the fund. APs are the mechanism that keeps an ETF's market price in line with its NAV — effectively the institutional plumbing behind every ETF.
Creation/Redemption: The process by which Authorized Participants deliver a basket of the underlying securities to the fund in exchange for new ETF shares (creation), or hand back ETF shares for the underlying basket (redemption). This mechanism is what keeps ETF prices tightly tethered to NAV.
Correlation: How closely two funds' returns move together, from −1 (perfectly opposite) to +1 (move identically). Two highly correlated funds (like VOO and IVV) offer little diversification benefit when held together.
Implied Volatility: The options market's forward-looking estimate of how volatile the underlying is expected to be, derived from options prices. Higher IV means pricier options and a market expecting bigger moves ahead.
Open Interest: The number of outstanding options contracts at a given strike/expiration that haven't been closed. Higher open interest generally signals a more liquid, actively used options market.
Put/Call Ratio: The ratio of put option volume (bets on/hedges against a decline) to call option volume (bets on a rise). A rough sentiment gauge — elevated put/call ratios can indicate hedging demand or bearish positioning.
Sector Weighting: The % of the fund allocated to each economic sector (technology, financials, healthcare, etc.). Determines what really drives the fund's returns — two funds can hold different companies but behave similarly if their sector mix overlaps heavily.
Holdings: The individual securities (stocks, bonds) the fund actually owns. Free data sources typically only disclose a fund's largest ~10 holdings by weight, not the full constituent list, which can run into the hundreds for broad index funds.
YTD: Year-to-date — the return from January 1st of the current year through today.
Basis Point: One-hundredth of one percent (0.01%). Fees and yield differences are usually quoted in basis points (bps) because the numbers involved are so small — a 3 bps fee is 0.03%.
Alpha: The excess return a fund generates beyond what its beta would predict given the market's move. Positive alpha means it beat its risk-adjusted expectation; for passive index funds, alpha should hover near zero minus fees, by design.
Liquidity: How easily and cheaply an asset can be bought or sold without moving its price. Driven by trading volume, bid-ask spread, and (for ETFs) the depth of the creation/redemption mechanism via Authorized Participants.
Market Maker: A firm that continuously quotes both buy and sell prices for a security, providing liquidity and profiting from the spread. Many Authorized Participants also act as market makers in the ETF's shares on-exchange.
Factor Tilt: A fund's systematic lean toward a specific style of stock — value, growth, quality, momentum, size — relative to the broad market. Explains why, say, a growth-tilted fund underperforms in rising-rate environments even while holding "good" companies.
Overlap: The percentage of two funds' holdings (by weight) that are identical. High overlap between two funds you hold means less real diversification than the fund count suggests.
Risk-Free Rate: The theoretical return on an investment with zero risk, typically proxied by short-term US Treasury bill yields. Used as the baseline in risk-adjusted return metrics like the Sharpe ratio.
Benchmark Index: The index a fund is designed to track (e.g. the S&P 500 for VOO). Performance and tracking error are measured relative to this target.
ETF: Exchange-Traded Fund — a basket of securities that trades on an exchange like a single stock, combining a mutual fund's diversification with a stock's intraday tradability and (usually) lower cost.
